title: JESUS KNELT TO WASH FEET. SO WHY DO SOME CHRISTIAN LEADERS DEMAND A THRONE?
paragraphs: JESUS KNELT TO WASH FEET. SO WHY DO SOME CHRISTIAN LEADERS DEMAND A THRONE?
The King of Heaven Wrapped a Towel Around His Waist—And Exposed Everything Wrong With Leadership That Wants to Be Worshiped Instead of Serving.
What if one of the most uncomfortable questions Jesus could ask the modern Church is this: “Why are you demanding the treatment I willingly gave up?”

Imagine walking into a church where the pastor's arrival causes everyone to stand. Someone rushes to carry his Bible. Another makes sure his special chair is ready. People carefully choose their words because questioning him might be interpreted as questioning God.
He is surrounded by people who call him anointed.
But some of those same people are afraid to tell him the truth.

A struggling widow sits quietly in the back, wondering how she will feed her children tomorrow. A young believer is wrestling with sin but is terrified of being judged. A volunteer who has served faithfully for years is exhausted, overlooked, and afraid that saying no will make them seem spiritually rebellious.
And somewhere in the middle of all that religious activity, a disturbing question begins to rise.
When did following the Servant King become an excuse to build a kingdom around the servant?

Before anyone becomes defensive, this is not an attack on pastors. There are faithful shepherds who pray when nobody sees, sacrifice without recognition, visit hospital rooms, comfort grieving families, and carry burdens their congregations will never fully understand.
Scripture commands believers to respect faithful spiritual leaders, recognize their labor, and support those who teach God's Word (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13; 1 Timothy 5:17–18).
But Scripture never commands believers to treat a pastor as though he were Jesus.
And there is a difference between honoring a shepherd and placing him on a throne.
To understand that difference, we must enter one of the most breathtaking scenes in the Gospel of John.
Not a cathedral.
Not a palace.
Not a conference filled with applause.
An upper room.
A table.
Twelve disciples.
And a basin of water.
The night before the crucifixion, Jesus knew exactly what was coming.
He knew the betrayal was already taking shape. He knew Peter would deny Him. He knew the disciples would scatter when fear overwhelmed their promises.
And He knew something else.
John 13:3 tells us that Jesus knew the Father had given all things into His hands, that He had come from God, and that He was returning to God.
Do not rush past that.
Jesus knew He possessed supreme authority. And what did He do with that authority?
He got up from supper.
He laid aside His outer garments.
He took a towel.
He wrapped it around Himself.
He poured water into a basin.
Then the Lord of glory knelt before His disciples and began washing their feet.
The hands that formed creation were now cleaning the dirt from human skin.
The One whom angels worshiped was performing the work of a servant.
The One who had every right to receive honor was demonstrating what holy authority looks like when it is governed by love.
And perhaps the most devastating detail is this:
Jesus knew Judas was going to betray Him. Yet the passage presents the foot-washing as extending to His disciples without recording Judas as an exception.
Think about that.
Jesus did not need to be ignorant of someone's betrayal to love him.
He did not surrender His holiness by serving a sinner.
He did not become less divine by stooping low.
He revealed the character of divine love.
John introduces this scene with a remarkable statement:
“Having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end.” — John 13:1, KJV
The Greek phrase is εἰς τέλος (eis telos).
It can carry the sense of loving to the end, and in this context it also communicates the fullness of Christ's persevering love.
Jesus was not performing a public relations gesture.
He was loving His own as the hour of His suffering approached.
He was showing them the kind of love that would soon take Him to the cross.
And suddenly the towel becomes more than a towel.
It becomes a visible rebuke to every form of spiritual pride that uses authority to demand admiration while refusing humble service.
Because the King who deserved everything chose to serve.
And some of us who deserve nothing have become offended when nobody treats us as important.
That should trouble every Christian.
Not only pastors.
All of us.
The worship leader who becomes angry when someone else receives an opportunity.
The ministry worker who serves faithfully until nobody notices.
The Bible teacher who cannot accept correction.
The church member who demands recognition because of years of giving.
The believer who quotes Scripture about humility while secretly craving a position above others.
Pride does not always wear expensive clothing.
Sometimes it wears a ministry badge.
Sometimes it carries a Bible.
Sometimes it stands behind a pulpit.
And sometimes it sits in the congregation, silently judging everyone else.
The frightening thing about spiritual pride is that it can make us feel close to God while making us increasingly unlike Christ.
Then Peter speaks.
When Jesus approaches him, Peter cannot understand what is happening.
“Lord, dost thou wash my feet?” — John 13:6, KJV
His response is understandable.
This is his Master.
His Teacher.
His Lord.
And now that Lord is kneeling before him.
Peter protests.
“Thou shalt never wash my feet.” — John 13:8, KJV
But Jesus answers:
“If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.” — John 13:8, KJV
There is something deeper here than an example of good leadership.
Jesus is teaching Peter that discipleship begins with receiving what only Christ can give.
Peter cannot cleanse himself into fellowship with Jesus.
He must allow the Savior to serve him.
The washing of feet becomes a profound picture of the cleansing and fellowship that come through Christ, even as the immediate scene also prepares the disciples to serve one another.
And this is where the Gospel confronts our pride from another direction.
Some people are too proud to serve.
Others are too proud to be served.
Some refuse to kneel because they believe they are above everyone else.
Others refuse to admit their need because they cannot bear to appear weak.
But the Gospel humbles both.
Before you can faithfully carry Christ's towel, you must acknowledge your need for Christ's cleansing.
You are not saved because you volunteered in church.
You are not forgiven because you gave money.
You are not justified because you respected your pastor.
You are not accepted by God because you served until your body was exhausted.
You are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ, whose death and resurrection accomplish what our religious performance never could (Ephesians 2:8–10; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And when that grace truly reaches the heart, it changes how we treat people.
Especially people who cannot offer us anything in return.
That brings us to the words every Christian leader should read slowly.
After Jesus finishes washing their feet, He puts His garments back on, returns to His place, and asks:
“Know ye what I have done to you?” — John 13:12, KJV
Imagine the silence.
Imagine the disciples looking at one another.
Imagine the embarrassment of realizing that the One they called Lord had just done something they themselves might have considered beneath them.
Then Jesus explains:
“Ye call me Master and Lord: and ye say well; for so I am.” — John 13:13, KJV
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not deny His authority.
He does not pretend that every role in the community is identical.
He does not suggest that leadership, teaching, or spiritual responsibility are unnecessary.
He affirms that He is their Teacher and Lord.
But then He reveals what His authority means for their behavior.
“If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet.” — John 13:14, KJV
In the Greek text, the phrase ὀφείλετε ἀλλήλων νίπτειν τοὺς πόδας (opheilete allēlōn niptein tous podas) communicates an obligation to wash one another's feet.
The word ὀφείλετε (opheilete) expresses what is owed or required.
Jesus is not merely recommending humility as an attractive personality trait.
He is placing His followers under an obligation to love and serve one another.
The Lord who washed their feet has established the pattern.
And nobody who claims to represent Him has the authority to reverse that pattern.
Christian leadership is not permission to rise above the people Christ calls us to love. It is a responsibility to care for them in His name.
That does not mean a pastor must literally wash everyone's feet every Sunday.

Some Christian traditions practice foot-washing as an ordinance or meaningful expression of obedience. Others understand Jesus' instruction primarily as a command to practice humble, practical service.
Faithful Christians differ on that application.
But the central meaning is unmistakable.
The disciple is not greater than the Master.
And the servant does not become too important to serve.
Jesus makes that explicit:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord; neither he that is sent greater than he that sent him.” — John 13:16, KJV
The Greek word δοῦλος (doulos) refers to a servant or slave.
In this saying, Jesus confronts the absurdity of a disciple imagining himself above the Lord whose example he is commanded to follow.
If Jesus did not consider humble service beneath Him, how can His followers consider it beneath them?
That question should echo through every church office.
Every leadership conference.
Every ministry boardroom.
Every Christian household.
And every heart that has ever confused spiritual responsibility with personal superiority.
Because there is a particular danger when religious authority becomes wrapped in the language of God's approval.
A leader can begin believing that disagreement is rebellion.
That correction is persecution.
That financial questions are attacks against the anointing.
That accountability is disrespect.
That ordinary people should sacrifice endlessly while leaders remain beyond scrutiny.
But the New Testament does not present church leadership as unquestionable royalty.
Peter himself later writes to the elders:
The Greek expression μηδ᾽ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες (mēd' hōs katakyrieuontes) warns against domineering leadership.
It is the language of exercising mastery over others, not shepherding them through godly example.
And that distinction matters enormously.
A shepherd protects the sheep.
A tyrant protects his position.
A shepherd teaches the truth.
A tyrant punishes uncomfortable questions.
A shepherd welcomes appropriate accountability.
A tyrant makes accountability seem sinful.
A shepherd cares about wounded people.
A tyrant cares primarily about whether those people remain useful.
Yet even here, we must be careful.
Not every wealthy pastor is corrupt.
Not every leader who receives an honorarium is greedy.
Not every church that provides transportation, housing, security, or administrative assistance to its ministers is practicing unbiblical favoritism.
Scripture explicitly teaches that those who labor in preaching and teaching may receive material support (1 Timothy 5:17–18; 1 Corinthians 9:14).
The issue is not whether a minister receives help.
The issue is whether that minister has begun treating God's people as instruments of personal privilege.
Biblical honor supports faithful service. Spiritual idolatry makes a human leader untouchable.
And the difference becomes painfully clear when someone gets hurt.
Consider the church member who approaches a leader privately about a serious concern.
She is trembling.
She has prayed for weeks.
She has struggled to find the courage to speak.
She does not want to destroy the church.
She loves the church.
That is precisely why she came.
But instead of receiving a patient hearing, she is told that questioning leadership is questioning God.
Now she leaves carrying two wounds.
The original concern.
And the fear that seeking truth has made her disloyal to Jesus.
If that has ever happened to you, hear this carefully.
Respecting spiritual authority does not require surrendering biblical discernment.

Scripture calls believers to test teaching (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1), address sin responsibly (Matthew 18:15–17), and handle accusations against elders with both fairness and seriousness (1 Timothy 5:19–20).
A faithful leader should not be condemned by rumors.
But neither should a leader be protected from legitimate examination merely because he occupies a pulpit.
God's Word protects truth, justice, and the flock.
Not the reputation of a powerful person at any cost.
And if you are a pastor reading this, please do not hear only accusation.
Hear an invitation.
The Lord who called you to shepherd His people has not asked you to become their savior.
You are allowed to be human.
You are allowed to be tired.
You are allowed to need encouragement.
You are allowed to receive support.
You are allowed to admit when you are wrong.
In fact, your willingness to repent may teach your congregation more about grace than a hundred sermons designed to make you appear flawless.
Your people do not need a pastor who never needs mercy.
They need a shepherd who knows where mercy is found.
And if you have been wounded by a leader, do not confuse the failures of that leader with the character of Jesus.
A pastor may have used authority to silence you.
Jesus used His authority to serve.
A religious institution may have treated you as disposable.
Jesus demonstrated a love that went all the way to the cross.
A leader may have demanded loyalty while refusing accountability.
Jesus, though sinless, willingly humbled Himself for the salvation of sinners.
Human representatives can misrepresent Christ.
But their failures do not change who Christ is.
The hands that some leaders use to point at their own importance are not the hands that saved you. The hands that saved you were pierced.
There is another scene in the Gospels that makes the contrast even sharper.
In Mark 10, James and John seek prominent places in Jesus' glory.
They want honor.
Recognition.
Positions of distinction.
And Jesus tells His disciples that worldly rulers exercise power over others, but His followers must not imitate that model.
“Whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister.” — Mark 10:43, KJV
The Greek word translated “minister” is διάκονος (diakonos), meaning servant or one who ministers.
Then Jesus reveals the foundation beneath His command:
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” — Mark 10:45, KJV
This is the heart of everything.
Jesus did not merely come to demonstrate an admirable leadership technique.
He came to give His life as a ransom.
His humility was not a performance.
His service was not a branding strategy.
His sacrifice was not a way to attract followers who would finance His comfort.
He came to accomplish redemption.
The cross is not simply the greatest example of selflessness.
It is the place where the sinless Savior gave Himself for sinners.
And that changes everything.
Because the problem with the human heart runs deeper than leadership style.
We want to be important.
We want to be admired.
We want our sacrifices noticed.
We want our opinions treated as unquestionable.
We want the benefits of Christ's kingdom without always accepting the humility of its King.
Even when we condemn pride in others, we can secretly nourish the same pride within ourselves.
That is why the Gospel does not simply tell arrogant people to behave better.
It calls sinners to repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
It announces forgiveness through His blood.
It promises new life through His resurrection.
It teaches us to die to selfish ambition and walk by the Spirit.
And it reminds us that genuine transformation is not accomplished by shame alone, but by the grace and power of God.
Paul writes:
The passage continues by describing Christ's humility, obedience, and death on the cross.
One of its central Greek expressions is ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτόν (etapeinōsen heauton).
“He humbled himself.” — Philippians 2:8, KJV
Jesus did not lose His divine identity when He humbled Himself.
He willingly took the position of a servant and became obedient unto death.
And the Father highly exalted Him.
This is not a promise that humble Christians will become celebrities.
It is a revelation of Christ's unique obedience and exaltation, and a call for believers to adopt His self-giving mind.
The Christian life does not revolve around manufacturing our own greatness.
It revolves around belonging to the One who is truly great.
So perhaps the question is no longer simply why some Christian leaders expect royal treatment.
Perhaps the deeper question is:
Why do so many of us still want a crown before we are willing to carry a towel?
What happens when nobody applauds your generosity?
When someone else receives the position you wanted?
When you are asked to serve people who cannot advance your reputation?
When a struggling believer needs your patience more than your advice?
When your spouse needs an apology instead of another explanation?
When your children need your presence more than your public image?
When a fellow Christian corrects you using Scripture?
When repentance would cost you the admiration of people who think you can do no wrong?
Those are not glamorous moments.
Nobody may photograph them.
Nobody may invite you onto a stage to talk about them.
But they are precisely the kinds of moments in which Christlike humility becomes visible.
And here is something worth remembering:
The towel is not a prop for proving how humble you are. It is a reminder that love must become action.
You can post about servant leadership and still mistreat the people closest to you.
You can preach John 13 and still refuse to apologize.
You can wash someone's feet in a public ceremony and still humiliate them behind closed doors.
You can speak beautifully about sacrifice while expecting others to make every sacrifice for you.
Jesus did not say His disciples would be blessed merely because they understood His teaching.
He said:
“If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them.” — John 13:17, KJV
The Greek word translated “happy” is μακάριοί (makarioi), commonly rendered “blessed.”
The blessing Jesus speaks of is connected to actually doing what He has taught.
Knowing is not the same as obeying.
Admiring humility is not the same as practicing it.
Quoting Jesus is not the same as following Jesus.
And the Church desperately needs that distinction.
We do not need less biblical respect for pastors.
We need more biblical respect for Christ.
We do not need to despise spiritual leadership.
We need leaders whose authority is exercised under the authority of Scripture.
We do not need congregations that treat every pastor with suspicion.
We need congregations that practice discernment without abandoning love.
We do not need to replace one personality cult with another.
We need to return to the crucified and risen Savior who alone deserves our worship.
And perhaps, somewhere tonight, a pastor is reading this while sitting alone after a difficult Sunday.
He remembers when ministry was simpler.
When he first preached, he was overwhelmed that God would use someone like him.
He did not dream about status.
He dreamed about seeing people come to Christ.
He wanted to teach the Bible faithfully.
He wanted to care for souls.
But slowly, ministry became tangled with expectations, comparison, influence, money, pressure, and the fear of losing respect.
He began protecting his image.
He stopped listening to correction.
He became irritated by ordinary people with ordinary problems.
And somewhere along the way, the towel disappeared.
If that is you, the invitation is not to despair.
It is to repent.
Christ is not calling you to manufacture a perfect public image.
He is calling you back to Himself.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Seek accountability.
Listen to those you have hurt.
Return to the Word.
Remember the wonder of the Gospel that first brought you to your knees.
The Savior who washed His disciples' feet still calls His people to humble obedience.
And His grace is not too small to transform a proud heart.
Perhaps another reader is remembering a church where they once felt safe.
You trusted the people there.
You served.
You gave.
You prayed.
You defended the leadership when others raised concerns.
Then something happened that shattered your confidence.
Now even hearing the word “church” makes your chest tighten.
You still believe in Jesus, but you struggle to trust anyone who claims to speak for Him.
Your pain deserves to be taken seriously.
And healing does not require pretending the wrong was acceptable.
Forgiveness does not automatically mean restoring someone to a position of trust.
Reconciliation, where possible, requires truth and genuine repentance.
Accountability is not the enemy of grace.
Sometimes it is one of the ways truth and love begin repairing what sin has damaged.
But please remember this.
The Jesus of John 13 is not standing over you demanding that you protect an institution at the expense of truth.
He is the Lord who knelt.
The Lord who served.
The Lord who loved His own to the end.
And the Lord who went to the cross.
Do not allow a human being's misuse of His name to become the final word about His character.
Let Jesus Himself show you who He is.
This is why the message of Gospel Warrior matters so deeply to us.
Not because we have built a perfect ministry.
Not because our voices deserve unquestioning loyalty.
But because the Word of God must remain greater than the personalities who proclaim it.
We want to keep pointing people back to Scripture, to repentance, to grace, to forgiveness, and above all, to Jesus Christ.
If this article has helped you examine your heart, understand Scripture more clearly, or find the courage to return to Christ, consider helping this message reach someone else.
Not to shame every pastor.
Not to provoke unnecessary division.
But because someone you know may be confusing loyalty to a leader with loyalty to Jesus.
Someone may need the courage to practice humble leadership.
Someone may need to know that spiritual abuse is not the character of Christ.
Someone may need to remember that even after religious disappointment, the Gospel is still good news.
Maybe your response is a testimony of a pastor who served your family in secret.
Maybe it is a confession that you have wanted recognition more than obedience.
Maybe it is a quiet request for prayer because you are still healing from church hurt.
There is no need to expose private wounds publicly. But your honest reflection may encourage someone who thought they were struggling alone.
And if you believe this ministry is helping people encounter the truth of God's Word, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from pressure.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
You do not have to give money to prove your love for Jesus.
And you do not have to purchase access to His grace.
Those free resources are part of the mission: helping people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and become more firmly rooted in Christ.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The Word of God must never become a tool for manipulating people's generosity.
And a ministry that teaches servant leadership must be willing to practice it in the way it asks for support.
That is part of what makes John 13 so powerful.
It does not allow us to preach humility to others while exempting ourselves.
It calls the preacher and the congregation.
The giver and the receiver.
The leader and the follower.
The wounded and the one who must repent.
All of us.
Back to Jesus.
Back to the basin.
Back to the towel.
Back to the cross.
Because the final answer to spiritual pride is not finding a more impressive religious personality.
It is beholding the Savior who had all authority and still chose to kneel.
The world may measure greatness by how many people stand when you enter a room.
Jesus showed His disciples a different kind of greatness.
One that bends down.
One that loves sacrificially.
One that tells the truth.
One that refuses to use people as stepping stones toward personal glory.
And one that ultimately leads us to the cross, where the sinless Son of God gave His life for sinners.
So before we ask why some Christian leaders expect to be treated like royalty, let every one of us ask a more personal question.
If Jesus walked into my life today carrying a towel, would He find me serving others—or demanding that others serve me?
That question is not meant to leave us hopeless.
It is meant to bring us to repentance.
Because the same Jesus who exposes our pride also offers forgiveness.
The same Jesus who commands us to serve also supplies grace for transformed living.
And the same Jesus who knelt before His disciples is now the risen and exalted Lord, worthy of every knee bowing before Him (Philippians 2:9–11).
His humility never diminished His glory.
It revealed the depth of His love.
And His glory never made Him indifferent to our need.
That is the King we follow.
Not a king who demands that wounded sinners build his reputation.
But the King who gave Himself to redeem them.
The most dangerous throne in the Church may be the one we have quietly built inside our own hearts—and the only King who can save us from it is the One who first knelt with a towel.
